Metafractal: The Space of Fractals Is Fractal

Every fractal is a point in a space of fractals. That space has its own roughness, its own coastlines and its own copies of itself, and it can be walked like a landscape.

iori1

1Jorik Jonathan Chase, 3DIE — Design, Art & Technologies Label. Paper 0.1 of a series, a companion to paper 0. October 2026.

The paper in one paragraph

A fractal made by a formula depends on numbers: change one and the shape changes. The set of all those shapes is a space, and this paper is about its geometry. In the plane the question has a famous answer. The Mandelbrot set is the map of the Julia sets: each of its points stands for one Julia set, and whether that point is inside the map says whether its Julia set is in one piece or scattered dust. The map is itself a fractal, and near special points it looks exactly like the shape it stands for. The space of these fractals is fractal. In three and four dimensions there is no such theorem, but there is an instrument. The Fractal Engine draws the map of any two parameters of any formula, measures how far each parameter moves the surface on screen, marks where the space turns chaotic, and walks it: breeding, mixing species inside the iteration, laying different formulas across space, and placing a map of families under the hand. The figures are the engine itself.

The first two figures are drawn in the page: move the crosshair, turn the zoom. The rest are the engine, started when they scroll into view; click or tap one to take the controls, press outside to give the page back its scroll. Nothing you do there is saved. The mathematics sits folded in boxes marked The mathematics. The engine's own documentation is The Fractal Engine, Tool by Tool.

1. The Mandelbrot Set Is a Map

Every point of the Mandelbrot set is a whole fractal, and the set says which of those fractals are in one piece.

Take the rule z → z² + c in the complex plane and fix c. Follow every starting point z: some fly off to infinity, some stay bounded forever. The boundary between the two is the Julia set of c, a fractal for almost every c [1] [2]. Now turn the question around: let c vary. The plane of all c is a space of Julia sets, one at each point.

Julia and Fatou found that only one orbit decides the shape: the orbit of 0, the point where z² folds the plane. If 0 stays bounded, the Julia set is connected, one piece. If 0 escapes, the Julia set falls apart into dust, uncountably many points with nothing between them. The Mandelbrot set is the set of c for which 0 stays bounded [3]. So it is a map in the plainest sense: one picture in which every point stands for a fractal, coloured by the one property that matters most. Douady and Hubbard proved the map itself is connected [4].

The mathematics

For fc(z) = z² + c, the filled Julia set Kc is the set of z whose orbit stays bounded, and the Julia set Jc = ∂Kc. The dichotomy (Fatou 1919, Julia 1918): Jc is connected if the critical orbit fcn(0) is bounded, and a Cantor set otherwise. Hence

M = { c : fcn(0) bounded } = { c : Jc connected }.

An orbit that leaves the disc |z| ≤ 2 never returns, which is the escape test both panes use.

2. The Map Looks Like What It Maps

Zoom into the Mandelbrot set at the right point and you see the Julia set that point stands for. The space of these fractals contains pictures of its own contents.

At a Misiurewicz point, a c whose critical orbit lands on a repelling cycle without being on it, Tan Lei proved that the Mandelbrot set and the Julia set of c become the same shape as you zoom in, up to a turn and a scale [5]. At c = i the Julia set is a dendrite, a tree of hairline branches; the Mandelbrot set near i is the same tree. The map, read closely, draws the territory.

Two more results make the space rough in the sense of paper 0. Shishikura proved the boundary of the Mandelbrot set has Hausdorff dimension 2, as rough as a curve can be [6]. And McMullen proved it is universal: small copies of the Mandelbrot set appear in the parameter space of every family of maps where a cycle can change its stability, so any space of fractals rich enough to bifurcate is rough in the same way [7].

The mathematics

Let c be a Misiurewicz point: fck(0) lies on a repelling cycle of period p and multiplier ρ, |ρ| > 1. Tan Lei (1990): there is λ ≠ 0 such that

limn→∞ ρn(M − c) = λ · limn→∞ ρn(Jc − c),

both limits taken in the Hausdorff metric on compact sets of a disc. Both sets are asymptotically self-similar about c with the same ratio ρ, and they agree up to the similarity λ. Shishikura (1998): dimH ∂M = 2. McMullen (2000): in any holomorphic family of rational maps, the bifurcation locus contains quasiconformal copies of ∂M, or of its higher-degree analogues.

3. Every Formula Has Its Map

There is no theorem for the Mandelbox. There is an instrument: the engine draws the map of any two parameters around the point you hold.

A Mandelbox or a Mandelbulb is built the way the Mandelbrot set is: iterate a rule, add the starting point back each time, ask what stays bounded. Fix the added constant instead and you get a Julia-type shape. The engine's push mode does exactly that for whatever point you look at, so one formula gives the Mandelbrot-type cave and, at every place in it, its own Julia-type cloud [8] [9].

The complex-analytic theorems do not reach these maps: folds and triplex powers are not holomorphic. What the engine offers instead is the atlas lens. Hold a point of the surface; the view becomes the plane of two of the formula's parameters around their current values, each pixel coloured by how far the surface would be from the held point under that pair. It is the held point's own Mandelbrot set: where the key colour runs, a parameter pair puts the surface back on your point, and the edges of that region are as rough as the parameter space is.

The mathematics

For a formula Fθ with distance estimate dθ, and a held point x0, the lens draws

(θ1, θ2) ↦ dθ(x0) / pixel,

over the window θ0 ± (screen size) / m, with m the metric of section 4. Its zero set is the set of parameters whose surface passes through x0, the analogue of M as the set of c whose critical orbit stays bounded. It is evaluated by the same shader that draws the field, so it is exact, not a sketch.

4. A Ruler on the Space, and Where It Turns Chaotic

To walk a space you need distances. The engine measures them in pixels on screen.

A number in a formula is not a distance: moving the Mandelbox's sphere radius by 0.01 changes the picture far more than moving its scale by 0.01. The engine follows every orbit together with its derivative with respect to one parameter (dual numbers) and turns that into how many pixels the surface moves per unit of the parameter, at every point it can see [10]. That is a metric on the space of fractals, local to the view: a step of 3 pixels moves the surface about 3 pixels, whichever number moves.

The same derivative gives the Lyapunov exponent, the rate at which nearby orbits part [11]. Where it is high, the space is about to change character: a small move of a parameter will change the picture a lot. Those are the coastlines of the space. The same phenomenon has been measured in machine learning: the boundary between hyperparameters that train and those that diverge is fractal [12].

The mathematics

At a surface point x seen through a pixel of footprint ε(x), the speed of parameter θ is

mθ(x) = |∂d/∂θ| / ( |∇d| · ε(x) )  pixels per unit,

the normal speed of the surface over the pixel size. The view's metric is the RMS over a grid of hits, a diagonal approximation of the pull-back of screen distance onto parameter space. The Lyapunov exponent is λ = lim (1/n) Σ log |J(pi)vi| along the orbit.

5. Walking the Space

With a ruler, the space can be explored at known distances and mapped by what it contains.

The engine's breed ring offers eight neighbours of the formula on screen: four at 35, 60, 90 and 130 pixels in random directions of the metric, and four from an archive that grows in the background. The archive is a MAP-Elites grid: the space is binned by two features you can see (how much of the view is surface, how chaotic it is) and the best formula found for each bin is kept [13]. It is a coarse chart of the neighbourhood, built by walking it. Choosing a neighbour walks there at constant visual speed, so the walk itself is a path through the space drawn frame by frame.

6. Between Families

Parameters move within one family. To cross from family to family the space needs new points, and the engine makes them three ways.

Chimeras. Two formulas run on the same point in the same iteration, and the point is blended between them. The result belongs to neither family: it is a new species with dynamics of its own, a point of the space that lies between two families rather than inside one.

Tissue. The blend weight can vary across space. In Voronoi tissue each cell of space is its own species, with soft walls between them, so one shape is a field over the space of fractals: every place a different formula [14].

The Metasurface. Eleven families laid out as Voronoi cells on a square: a chart of the space of families under the hand. Inside a cell, the crosshair breeds the family along its own two axes; across a wall, the families blend, by parameters when they share a structure and as a chimera when they do not [15]. A stroke across the square is a path through the space, played in time or laid out in space.

The mathematics

A chimera of FA and FB with weight field ω is the map p ↦ (1 − ω)FA(p) + ωFB(p). For constant ω it is a path in the space of maps between the two families; ω ∈ {0, 1} returns each. The Metasurface's weights are πj ∝ exp(−(dj − dmin)/0.035) over the distances to the sites, so the chart is pure in each cell and continuous across every wall.

7. Proven, Observed, Open

The claim of the title is a theorem in the plane and an observation everywhere else.

  • Proven for z² + c: the map is connected (Douady, Hubbard), its boundary has dimension 2 (Shishikura), it looks like its Julia sets at Misiurewicz points (Tan Lei), and copies of it appear in every holomorphic family that bifurcates (McMullen).
  • Observed for the engine's formulas: the lens maps have rough edges at every zoom the shader can reach; the Lyapunov exponent is high in patches with sharp borders; the breed ring's neighbours at equal metric distance differ most where λ is high.
  • Open, and measurable with the engine: the box-counting dimension of a lens map's zero set, as paper 0 measured coastlines; whether that dimension depends on the formula or only on how chaotic it is; whether the 3-D families have points where the lens map and the Julia-type cloud agree, as Tan Lei's do.
